b: When I work out in the morning, there’s a group of elderly people who blab on and on. In the afternoon I’m slapped with a group of college kids who cackle like chickens.
Working out isn’t a social event! No smiling.
When I exercise, I look like the Unabomber. My hoodie is stained. I pull my hat down over my eyes. Don’t talk to me.
Today, I had a conversation with myself. It ended with, “Shut up unless you plan to do anything about it.”
Complaining makes me feel powerful. Standing aloof is easy joy.
Research indicates that 75% of complaints aren’t intended to change anything. We complain to vent or gain sympathy.
I hope you appreciate how horrible my life is.
People need to feel heard before they move forward.
Say: “I can see this matters to you.”
Sympathy is enough for some. Others want solutions.
Ask: “Would you like me to listen or would you like to figure out a solution?”
Complainers circle what’s wrong. Leaders work to make things better.
Ask: “What would you like to happen?”
Ask: “What part of this situation can you influence?”
Don’t train people to come to you with problems they should fix.
Ask: “What’s one step you’re willing to take?”
Dismissing complaints suggests you don’t care.
Demanding solutions you should provide. Remember, some concerns like harassment, safety violations, and unethical conduct require your attention.
Tomorrow I’ll pull my hat down and mind my own business. Probably.
What’s a leader-like response to complaining?
